questions.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of science?
options: To explain the natural world using evidence
To prove that old ideas are always wrong
To make guesses without testing them
questions.answer: To explain the natural world using evidence
questions.feedback: Science uses evidence from observations and investigations to explain the natural world.

questions.question: Which of these is most important when scientists make a claim?
questions.feedback: Scientific claims should be supported by evidence.

questions.question: Why do scientists repeat investigations?
options: To check whether results are reliable
questions.answer: To check whether results are reliable
questions.feedback: Repeating investigations helps scientists check the reliability of their results.

questions.question: What is a fair test?
options: An investigation where only one variable is changed at a time
An investigation where everything is changed
An investigation based only on guesses
questions.answer: An investigation where only one variable is changed at a time
questions.feedback: A fair test changes one variable and keeps other conditions controlled.

questions.question: Which object is at the centre of our Solar System?
questions.feedback: The Sun is the star at the centre of our Solar System.

questions.question: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: Earth moving closer to the Sun
questions.feedback: Day and night are caused by Earth rotating on its axis.

questions.question: Why are Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander astronomical knowledges important in science learning?
options: They show long-term observations of the sky and environment
They are only stories with no patterns
questions.answer: They show long-term observations of the sky and environment
questions.feedback: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander astronomical knowledges include careful observations of sky patterns and environmental changes.

questions.question: Which is an example of using sky observations in everyday life?
options: Using star patterns to support navigation or seasonal knowledge
Ignoring patterns in the night sky
Changing the length of a day
questions.answer: Using star patterns to support navigation or seasonal knowledge
questions.feedback: Sky observations can support navigation, seasonal knowledge and understanding environmental patterns.

questions.question: Why have models of the Universe changed over time?
options: New evidence and better technology have improved our understanding
questions.answer: New evidence and better technology have improved our understanding
questions.feedback: Scientific models can change when new evidence or better technology improves our understanding.

questions.question: Which tool has helped scientists observe distant objects in space?
questions.feedback: Telescopes help scientists observe distant objects in space.

questions.question: Which is a direct observation?
options: The Moon makes its own light.
The Moon is made of ice.
questions.feedback: An observation describes what was seen.

questions.question: Which instrument measures elapsed time?
questions.feedback: A stopwatch measures time intervals.

questions.question: What does a telescope collect to form an image of a distant star?
questions.feedback: Optical telescopes collect light.

questions.question: Which object orbits Earth naturally?
questions.feedback: The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite.

questions.question: Which object is a star?
questions.feedback: The Sun is a star.

questions.question: What does Earth orbit?
questions.feedback: Earth travels around the Sun.

questions.question: What is a galaxy?
options: A vast collection of stars, gas and dust
questions.answer: A vast collection of stars, gas and dust
questions.feedback: Galaxies contain many stars and other matter.

questions.question: Which object reflects sunlight to appear bright in our sky?
questions.feedback: Moonlight is mostly reflected sunlight.

questions.question: About how long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.feedback: One Earth orbit takes about one year.

questions.question: What is a constellation as seen from Earth?
options: A named pattern or region of the sky
A group of planets circling Earth
questions.answer: A named pattern or region of the sky
questions.feedback: Constellations organise the sky into recognisable regions.

questions.question: Why is the Sun easier to study in detail than other stars?
options: It is much closer to Earth.
It is the only star that gives off light.
It is bigger than every other star.
questions.answer: It is much closer to Earth.
questions.feedback: The Sun is our nearest star.

questions.question: Where should you record measurements from repeated observations?
questions.feedback: A table keeps observations organised.

questions.question: Which statement is an inference from seeing a tree shadow move?
options: The shadow was 25 cm long at noon.
The shadow lay west of the tree at 9 am.
The shadow crossed a chalk mark.
questions.feedback: An inference explains or interprets an observation.

questions.question: To compare how quickly two sites cool at night, what should match?
options: The measuring times and type of thermometer
questions.answer: The measuring times and type of thermometer
questions.feedback: Matching the method makes the sites easier to compare.

questions.question: Why include units with a shadow length?
options: So another person can interpret the measurement
So the shadow stays the same
So no repeat readings are needed
questions.answer: So another person can interpret the measurement
questions.feedback: A number alone does not tell the reader the measurement scale.

questions.question: Why does the Moon appear to change shape over a month?
options: We see different amounts of its sunlit half.
Earth’s shadow covers it every night.
It changes shape as it cools.
The Sun lights different physical sides permanently.
questions.answer: We see different amounts of its sunlit half.
questions.feedback: The viewing angle changes as the Moon orbits Earth.

questions.question: Why do stars appear to move across the sky during one night?
questions.feedback: Earth’s rotation changes the direction we face.

questions.question: Which model best represents a solar eclipse?
options: The Moon lies between the Sun and Earth.
Earth lies between the Sun and Moon.
The Sun lies between Earth and Moon.
questions.answer: The Moon lies between the Sun and Earth.
questions.feedback: The Moon blocks sunlight from reaching part of Earth.

questions.question: Which model best represents a lunar eclipse?
options: Earth lies between the Sun and Moon.
The Moon lies between Earth and the Sun.
The Sun lies between Earth and Moon.
The Moon moves inside Earth’s atmosphere.
questions.answer: Earth lies between the Sun and Moon.
questions.feedback: Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon.

questions.question: Why can Venus appear bright although it is a planet?
options: It reflects only light from Earth.
questions.feedback: Venus reflects sunlight, especially from its clouds.

questions.question: What improves when a telescope collects more light from a faint object?
options: The object can be detected more clearly.
questions.answer: The object can be detected more clearly.
questions.feedback: More collected light makes faint objects easier to detect.

questions.question: What is a respectful first step before sharing a community’s sky knowledge in class?
options: Consult the relevant knowledge holders and use approved material.
Assume the knowledge is identical across Australia.
Use an anonymous online retelling without checking it.
Combine unrelated stories into one account.
questions.answer: Consult the relevant knowledge holders and use approved material.
questions.feedback: Knowledge belongs in its community context and may have sharing protocols.

questions.question: Why might different communities use different seasonal sky indicators?
options: They observe from different places and relate the sky to local changes.
Only one community can observe stars correctly.
Stars shine only in one area.
Every seasonal indicator must use the same star.
questions.answer: They observe from different places and relate the sky to local changes.
questions.feedback: Local geography and seasonal events shape useful observations.

questions.question: A student records shadow length at 9 am, noon and 3 pm. What is the measured variable?
questions.feedback: Shadow length is the outcome being measured.

questions.question: What makes a claim about changing shadow length stronger?
options: Repeated measurements at the same times on comparable days
Removing readings that look unusual without checking
questions.answer: Repeated measurements at the same times on comparable days
questions.feedback: Repeats let students see whether the pattern is consistent.

questions.question: What happens to a stick’s shadow as the Sun gets higher in the sky?
options: It gets longer regardless of position.
questions.feedback: Higher-angle sunlight produces a shorter shadow on level ground.

questions.question: Why might a model of the Solar System use different scales for sizes and distances?
options: Using one scale can make either planets too small or distances too large to show.
Distances are the same for every planet.
One scale makes gravity stop working.
questions.answer: Using one scale can make either planets too small or distances too large to show.
questions.feedback: Sizes and distances differ so much that a single scale is often impractical.

questions.question: Which statement is a testable prediction?
options: If I observe at the same time tomorrow, the Moon will be farther east against the stars.
The Moon is the nicest object in the sky.
The stars should be brighter because I like them.
questions.answer: If I observe at the same time tomorrow, the Moon will be farther east against the stars.
questions.feedback: The first statement gives an outcome that can be checked.

questions.question: What made observations of moons orbiting Jupiter important to older models?
options: They showed that some objects orbit something other than Earth.
They proved Earth has no Moon.
They showed all stars orbit Jupiter.
They proved the Sun orbits Earth.
questions.answer: They showed that some objects orbit something other than Earth.
questions.feedback: Jupiter’s moons contradicted the idea that everything circles Earth.

questions.question: Shadow lengths at noon over three days are 21 cm, 22 cm and 61 cm. What should you do first?
options: Check the method and conditions for the 61 cm reading.
Delete it because it is different.
Conclude immediately that all shadows are getting longer.
questions.answer: Check the method and conditions for the 61 cm reading.
questions.feedback: Investigate an unusual result before deciding how to treat it.

questions.question: Earth rotated twice as fast but orbited at the same rate. What would change?
options: The day would be shorter and the year would stay about the same.
The year would halve and the day would stay the same.
questions.answer: The day would be shorter and the year would stay about the same.
questions.feedback: Rotation controls day length and orbit controls year length.

questions.question: Two stars look equally bright. What can you conclude from appearance alone?
options: They deliver similar apparent brightness, but may differ in distance or light output.
They must give off the same amount of light.
They must be in the same constellation.
questions.answer: They deliver similar apparent brightness, but may differ in distance or light output.
questions.feedback: Distance and light output both affect apparent brightness.

questions.question: Why is there usually no solar eclipse at new Moon?
options: The Moon’s tilted orbit usually carries it above or below the line to the Sun.
Earth casts its shadow at every new Moon.
The Sun is too far away for any eclipse.
questions.answer: The Moon’s tilted orbit usually carries it above or below the line to the Sun.
questions.feedback: An eclipse requires closer alignment than the ordinary new Moon phase.

questions.question: Why record observing location along with the time when comparing sky observations?
options: Observers at different locations can see different parts or positions of the sky.
The location changes how fast Earth rotates.
The location changes the star’s temperature.
Time is unnecessary if the location is known.
questions.answer: Observers at different locations can see different parts or positions of the sky.
questions.feedback: Location and time are both needed to interpret and reproduce observations.

questions.question: One clear night a student sees fewer stars from town than from a dark field. Which follow-up tests light pollution as an explanation?
options: Repeat at both sites under similar weather and Moon conditions.
Compare town during daytime with the field at night.
Count stars only next to the brightest town light.
Look from the field on a cloudy night.
questions.answer: Repeat at both sites under similar weather and Moon conditions.
questions.feedback: Matching other conditions helps isolate the effect of artificial lighting.

questions.question: Why can a spacecraft facing away from the Sun lose power from its solar panels?
options: The panels receive less direct sunlight.
There is no gravity behind the spacecraft.
The spacecraft moves outside the Solar System.
The Sun gives off sound instead of light.
questions.answer: The panels receive less direct sunlight.
questions.feedback: Solar panels need incoming light to generate electricity.

questions.question: A diagram draws the Moon larger than Earth for readability. What must the diagram say?
options: Object sizes are not to scale.
The Moon is larger than Earth.
Both objects are at the same distance from the Sun.
questions.answer: Object sizes are not to scale.
questions.feedback: A scale note prevents a misleading comparison.

questions.question: A community calendar links a seasonal sky event with a change on Country. What is a reasonable interpretation?
options: The sky event can be a seasonal indicator without causing the change.
The sky event must directly cause the change.
The indicator has the same meaning everywhere.
The calendar does not rely on observation.
questions.answer: The sky event can be a seasonal indicator without causing the change.
questions.feedback: Events can recur together because of seasonal cycles.

questions.question: How can the Moon be visible in daytime?
options: It can be above the horizon while reflecting sunlight.
It makes its own light only in daytime.
The Sun blocks all other objects but pushes the Moon into view.
It is only visible after sunset.
questions.answer: It can be above the horizon while reflecting sunlight.
questions.feedback: The Moon can share the daytime sky with the Sun.

questions.question: Two observing groups disagree about a planet’s apparent position. What should they compare first?
options: Observation time, location and the reference stars used
questions.answer: Observation time, location and the reference stars used
questions.feedback: Different times, locations or reference points can explain different observations.
